title: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE BECAUSE OF HARDNESS OF HEART—THEN POINTED BACK TO EDEN
paragraphs: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE BECAUSE OF HARDNESS OF HEART—THEN POINTED BACK TO EDEN
They asked Jesus when a marriage could be ended. Jesus answered by taking them back to why marriage existed before sin ever entered the world.
There are questions we ask because we desperately want truth.
And then there are questions we ask because we are hoping truth will give us permission.
The Pharisees came to Jesus carrying one of those questions.
“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for just any reason?”
It sounded theological.
It sounded like a debate about Moses.
But Jesus heard something underneath the question.
A human heart looking for the boundary.
How far can I go?
When am I allowed to walk away?
What is the minimum God requires of me?
Where is the loophole?
And instead of beginning with divorce...
Jesus began with Eden.
That should stop us.
Because when human beings wanted to discuss how a marriage could be dismantled, Jesus pointed them toward the moment marriage was created.
Matthew records the question this way:
“Εἰ ἔξεστιν ἀνθρώπῳ ἀπολῦσαι τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν;”
The heart of their question is essentially:
“Is it lawful for a man to release/divorce his wife for every cause?”
The Greek verb ἀπολῦσαι (apolysai) carries the sense of releasing, sending away, or divorcing.
But Jesus refuses to begin where they begin.
He says:
“Οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε...”
“Have you not read...?”
Then He reaches all the way back to creation.
Not merely to Moses.
Not merely to Deuteronomy.
Not merely to what fallen people were permitted to do in a broken world.
Back...
to the beginning.
Jesus recalls Genesis:
“ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτοὺς”
“Male and female He made them.”
Then:
“ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
“The two shall become one flesh.”
And then comes the sentence that changes the entire conversation:
“ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.”
“What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
Notice what Jesus just did.
They asked about permission.
Jesus spoke about purpose.
They asked about divorce.
Jesus spoke about creation.
They asked what a man was legally allowed to do.
Jesus reminded them of what God had done.
That difference matters.
Because the biblical vision of marriage does not begin with two people standing at an altar.
It begins with God.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
A man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
Basar echad.
בָשָׂר אֶחָד.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing a house.
Not merely two people sharing bills.
Not merely two people who once felt butterflies.
Not merely two people posting anniversary pictures while quietly becoming strangers behind closed doors.
One flesh.
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, reaches deeper than convenience.
Deeper than chemistry.
Deeper than romance.
It is covenantal union under God.
And that is exactly why what happens next is so uncomfortable.
The Pharisees push back.
If that is God's intention, they essentially ask, then why did Moses tell people to give a certificate of divorce?
Jesus answers:
“Μωϋσῆς πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν ἀπολῦσαι τὰς γυναῖκας ὑμῶν...”
“Moses, because of your hardness of heart, permitted you to divorce your wives...”
Then Jesus adds:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.”
“But from the beginning it has not been this way.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
Because one word changes everything.
Permitted.
The Greek is ἐπέτρεψεν—epetrepsen.
Permitted.
Jesus does not describe divorce here as the beautiful design God established in Eden.
He points to a concession associated with human brokenness.
And He names the disease beneath it:
σκληροκαρδία.
Sklerokardia.
Hardness of heart.
It is a brutal word because it does not allow us to keep every conversation safely outside ourselves.
We would rather discuss who was technically right.
Who started it.
Who apologized first.
Who failed more.
Who had biblical grounds.
Who said what.
Who signed what.
Who left whom.
Jesus goes deeper.
The heart.
Because before some marriages collapse publicly, something has often been hardening privately.
A heart stops listening.
A heart stops confessing.
A heart stops forgiving.
A heart starts keeping score.
A heart becomes comfortable with contempt.
A heart learns how to punish with silence.
A heart can sit beside someone in church, sing about grace, listen to a sermon about mercy...
and then go home unwilling to say,
“I was wrong.”
Hardness does not always arrive screaming.
Sometimes it arrives quietly.
One ignored wound.
One secret message.
One unconfessed resentment.
One flirtation justified as harmless.
One apology withheld because pride would rather win than reconcile.
One night sleeping back-to-back.
Then another.
Then another.
Until two people who once could not imagine life apart begin imagining peace only if the other person disappears.
And perhaps that is where this article found you.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful.
Guard it.
Do not wait for catastrophe before learning how to repent.
Do not wait for betrayal before establishing boundaries.
Do not wait until affection disappears before becoming intentional about tenderness.
Do not assume a wedding covenant survives automatically because wedding photographs still exist.
Bring your marriage continually under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
But perhaps you are reading this with tears already forming.
Maybe you know what it feels like to watch something sacred fracture.
Maybe you have been divorced.
Maybe someone abandoned you.
Maybe adultery shattered what you thought was safe.
Maybe you were the unfaithful one.
Maybe you were the hard-hearted one.
Maybe you begged someone to stay.
Maybe you were handed papers you never wanted.
Maybe there are children involved.
Maybe years have passed, but hearing the word “divorce” still makes something inside you ache.
Maybe your story is complicated enough that simplistic Christian slogans feel like another wound.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus' words about the sacredness of marriage were not spoken so Christians could weaponize them against wounded people.
They were spoken because covenant matters to God.
And the same Jesus who tells the truth about sin is the Jesus who receives sinners.

The church must never turn God's high view of marriage into permission to shame every divorced person as though every broken marriage has the same story, the same responsibility, or the same circumstances.
Scripture itself requires more careful pastoral wisdom than that.

Matthew 19 continues into Jesus' teaching concerning sexual immorality. Paul later addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Faithful Christians have debated aspects of divorce and remarriage for centuries, but none of those debates should erase the central force of Jesus' answer here:
God's design must not be reconstructed around the hardness of the human heart.
And neither should Jesus' teaching be twisted into demanding that someone quietly endure violence or immediate danger.
Protecting someone from harm is not the same thing as treating covenant casually.

If you are in danger, getting to safety and seeking trustworthy pastoral, professional, and legal help can be necessary. Reconciliation, where it is biblically and safely possible, requires truth and repentance; it is not pretending evil never happened.
Because biblical reconciliation is not merely returning to the same room.
It involves truth.
Repentance.
Grace.
Transformation.
And this is where Matthew 19 stops being merely an article about divorce.
It becomes an examination of us.
Because sklerokardia does not belong only in divorce court.
Hardness of heart can live inside a marriage that never legally ends.
It can live inside a church pew.
Inside a ministry.
Inside a preacher.
Inside the person sharing Bible verses every morning.
Inside you.
Inside me.
You can remain married and still have a hard heart.
You can know Scripture and have a hard heart.
You can defend biblical marriage while treating your own spouse with cruelty.
You can win theological arguments and lose tenderness.
You can expose everybody else's sin while protecting your own.
You can say “Jesus is Lord” and still have rooms inside your heart where Jesus is not allowed to touch anything.
That is why the deepest question is not merely:
“Have I ever been divorced?”
The deeper question is:
“Where has my heart become hard toward God?”
Where have you stopped listening?
What sin are you defending?
Whom have you refused to forgive?
What secret are you protecting?
What bitterness have you renamed “discernment”?
What pride have you renamed “standards”?
What lust have you renamed “needs”?
What selfishness have you renamed “self-care”?
What disobedience have you renamed “my truth”?
Jesus is not merely trying to improve marriages.
Jesus came to save sinners.
That includes husbands.
That includes wives.
That includes divorced people.
That includes people who have committed adultery.
That includes people who have been betrayed.
That includes people whose marriages survived.
That includes people whose marriages did not.
That includes people carrying consequences they cannot reverse.
That includes the person reading this thinking,
“If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same way.”
Jesus already knows.
And He went to the cross anyway.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin does not matter.
Grace would be meaningless if sin did not matter.
The scandal is that our sin mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed for it...
and His mercy is greater than the darkest chapter surrendered to Him.
At Calvary, Jesus did not call evil good.
He bore evil's judgment.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He was pierced because sin is deadly.
He did not lower God's holiness until sinners could reach it.
He came down to sinners, fulfilled righteousness, carried our guilt, died our death, and rose again.
So repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
It is the moment you stop defending what is killing you.
It is the moment you stop saying,
“But they did...”
and finally ask,
“Jesus, what has happened to my heart?”
Maybe your spouse needs repentance.
Maybe your former spouse needs repentance.
Maybe somebody who wounded you needs repentance.
But you cannot repent for them.
You can only bring your own heart before Christ.
And sometimes the bravest prayer in a marriage is not,
“Lord, change them.”
Sometimes it is:
“Lord...
start with me.”
Search me.
Break my pride.
Expose my selfishness.
Teach me to listen again.
Teach me to tell the truth.
Teach me to forgive without pretending sin does not matter.
Teach me to seek forgiveness without demanding instant trust.
Teach me to love as someone who has been loved by Christ.
Give me a heart of flesh again.
That language should sound familiar.
God promised in Ezekiel 36:26:
“וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת־לֵב הָאֶבֶן מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר”
God speaks of removing the “heart of stone” and giving a “heart of flesh.”
Think about that beside Matthew 19.
Jesus identifies hardness of heart.
The Gospel announces a Savior who does not merely command hard hearts to behave better.
He makes people new.
Christianity is not behavior modification with Bible verses attached.
It is resurrection.
It is the Holy Spirit invading places sin has made dead.
It is Christ taking people who have learned to hide, blame, manipulate, betray, lust, hate, withdraw, and destroy...
and teaching them another way to live.
That does not mean every broken marriage will be restored.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships cannot return to what they were.
Some people will refuse repentance.
Some wounds require enormous time.
Forgiveness does not automatically recreate trust, and reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one person's effort alone.
But no surrendered life is beyond the redeeming reach of Jesus Christ.
Your past may explain scars.
It does not have to become your god.
Your divorce does not have to become your identity.
Your betrayal does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your victimization does not have to become the final sentence over your life.
If you belong to Christ, the loudest name over you is not “divorced.”
Not “abandoned.”
Not “adulterer.”
Not “failure.”
Not “damaged.”
Not “unlovable.”
Christ has the final word over those who come to Him in repentant faith.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Being made new.
And maybe now we understand why Jesus went back to Eden.
He was doing more than winning an argument with Pharisees.
He was exposing the tragedy of sin.
Look at what God intended.
Then look at what hard hearts have done.
But do not stop there.
Look at Christ.
Because the Bible begins with a marriage in a garden...
and moves toward another wedding.
Christ and His redeemed people.
The Bridegroom who does not abandon His Bride because loving her became inconvenient.
The Bridegroom who loved His people sacrificially.
The Bridegroom who gave Himself for His church.
The Bridegroom whose covenant faithfulness exposes our faithlessness...
and whose grace is the only reason faithless sinners can ever come home.
So if your marriage is healthy, do not become proud.
Stay dependent on Christ.
If your marriage is struggling, do not wait until resentment has eaten everything tender.
Seek help.
Tell the truth.
Pray together.
Confess quickly.
Get wise biblical counsel.
Put the phone down.
Listen.
Repent.
Forgive.
Fight for holiness harder than you fight to be right.
If you have sinned sexually, stop hiding.
If you are emotionally involved with someone who is not your spouse, stop feeding the fantasy.
If pornography has invaded your covenant, drag it into the light.
If bitterness has become your daily bread, stop calling it protection.
If you are manipulating Scripture to control your spouse, repent.
If you have wounded someone, do not use grace as a shortcut around accountability.
And if you are the wounded one, remember that forgiveness does not require you to call evil good.
Bring everything into the light of Jesus.
Everything.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make our scandals less embarrassing.
He died and rose again to make sinners new.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior.
From scandal...
to grace.
Not because scandals are insignificant.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because Christians never fail spectacularly.
But because Jesus Christ still saves, forgives, restores, sanctifies, heals, disciplines, and transforms people who surrender themselves to Him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Talk to Jesus.
Right now.
Not as a performance.
Not so strangers will think you are spiritual.
Let it be a confession.
A small public declaration that you are finished pretending you have nothing left for Christ to change.
And if you have been hiding something that needs to come into the light, perhaps today your words are simply:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person fighting for faith.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may see your testimony months from now and realize failure does not have to be the final chapter.

Not because every sentence will be easy to hear, but because there may come a night when anger is louder than covenant, temptation is louder than wisdom, shame is louder than grace, or hopelessness tells you nothing can change.
Come back.
Read Matthew 19 again.
Remember Eden.
Remember the hard heart.
Then remember the cross.
But voluntary generosity is biblical.
Keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep putting Scripture in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something on their phone at 2:00 in the morning.
And sometimes...
that is where Jesus meets them.
The resources are important.
Bigger than numbers.
Bigger than algorithms.
Bigger than us.
We want Jesus Christ proclaimed.
We want Scripture opened.
We want sinners called to repentance.
We want ashamed people shown the cross.
We want wounded believers reminded that grace is not a theory.
We want marriages strengthened where restoration is possible.
We want hard hearts softened.
We want lost people found.
We want believers discipled.
We want Christ glorified.
Pray for the ministry.
Comment and help another person feel less alone.
Save the truth and return to it.
There are many ways to participate in spreading the Gospel, and none of us purchases God's favor.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
Maybe that is where this entire conversation finally lands.
The Pharisees came asking Jesus about the point at which a person could let someone go.
Jesus took them back to the God who joined them together.
They pointed to paperwork.
Jesus pointed to the heart.
They pointed to Moses.
Jesus pointed to Eden.
And eventually...
the story of Scripture points us to a cross.
Because our deepest problem has never merely been broken marriages.
It is broken hearts.
Hard hearts.
Sinful hearts.
Hearts that need more than advice.
More than rules.
More than religious appearances.
We need resurrection.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
So before you leave this page, ask yourself one question that no Pharisee asked that day:
“Jesus... where has my heart become hard?”
Do not answer quickly.
Let Him search you.
And whatever He reveals...
bring it into the light.
Because the heart that finally stops defending its hardness is the heart grace can begin transforming.
You may not be able to rewrite what happened yesterday—but when you surrender the pen, Jesus can still redeem what your story becomes tomorrow.
